en: Itivuttaka 67: Tikanipāta, Second Chapter Thus it was said by the Blessed One, so I have heard: “Monks, there are these three kinds of persons found existing in the world. What three? The person who is like a stone pillar, the person who is like a tree stump, and the person who is like a lotus. And how, monks, is one a person like a stone pillar? Here, monks, a certain person dwells with a mind full of hatred toward his mother, father, brothers, sisters, friends, companions, kinsmen, and relatives; he dwells with a mind full of hatred toward ascetics and brahmins. This, monks, is called a person like a stone pillar. And how, monks, is one a person like a tree stump? Here, monks, a certain person does not perform even a small act of merit, nor does he cause others to do so, nor does he rejoice in the merit performed by others. This, monks, is called a person like a tree stump. And how, monks, is one a person like a lotus? Here, monks, a certain person dwells with a mind free from hatred toward his mother, father, brothers, sisters, friends, companions, kinsmen, and relatives; he dwells with a mind free from hatred toward ascetics and brahmins. He performs even a small act of merit, and he causes others to do so, and he rejoices in the merit performed by others. This, monks, is called a person like a lotus. These, monks, are the three kinds of persons found existing in the world. Thus spoke the Blessed One. Having said this, the Well-Farer rose from his seat and entered his dwelling. Then, not long after the Blessed One had departed, a certain monk approached the Venerable Ānanda and said to him: “Venerable Ānanda, what is the meaning of ‘a person like a stone pillar,’ ‘a person like a tree stump,’ and ‘a person like a lotus’? “Friend, just as a stone pillar, though struck by rain, wind, and cold, remains unshaken and unmoved, so too, friend, when a person dwells with a mind full of hatred toward his mother, father, brothers, sisters, friends, companions, kinsmen, and relatives; when he dwells with a mind full of hatred toward ascetics and brahmins—this, friend, is called a person like a stone pillar. Just as a tree stump, friend, cannot be used for any purpose, so too, friend, when a person does not perform even a small act of merit, nor causes others to do so, nor rejoices in the merit performed by others—this, friend, is called a person like a tree stump. Just as a lotus flower, friend, though struck by rain, wind, and cold, remains unshaken and unmoved, so too, friend, when a person dwells with a mind free from hatred toward his mother, father, brothers, sisters, friends, companions, kinsmen, and relatives; when he dwells with a mind free from hatred toward ascetics and brahmins; when he performs even a small act of merit, causes others to do so, and rejoices in the merit performed by others—this, friend, is called a person like a lotus. Thus spoke the Venerable Ānanda. Those monks were satisfied and delighted by the words of the Venerable Ānanda.
The Discourse on the Ways of the Sage.
This was said by the Blessed One, said by the Arahant; thus have I heard:
"Monks, there are these three ways of the sage."
Purity of body, purity of speech, and purity of mind—
these, monks, are the three purities.”
The Blessed One spoke this matter.
“One who is silent in body, silent in speech,
The sage whose mind is silent and free from taints, who is perfected in sagacity—
they call him one who has washed away all evil.
This matter too was spoken by the Blessed One; thus have I heard.
